prompt: A subquery in the SELECT list, where one value is expected, matches two rows. What happens?
hint: One of the two failure modes is loud and the other is silent.

choices.why: A scalar position takes a value; it has no way to become two rows.
No engine concatenates on your behalf, and the types would rarely allow it.

choices.text: The query fails with an error
choices.why: The database refuses rather than picking one, and tells you an assumption was wrong.
Picking silently is what you would want to be warned about, so nobody does it.

prompt: The same subquery matches no rows at all. What happens then?
hint: Compare it with what two rows did.

choices.why: A subquery in the SELECT list produces a value and decides nothing about rows.
Quietly, with no message, and lesson 4's section about unknowns then applies to it.
Substituting a zero would be a claim about the data that nobody made.

choices.text: An error, as with two rows
choices.why: Too many rows is checked; too few is a perfectly ordinary empty result.

prompt: Why does a subquery in FROM need an alias?
hint: Think about how you would write one of its columns in the outer query.

choices.text: The planner reads it to plan
choices.why: The decision is made from the shape of the query, and a name carries no hint.

choices.text: Without one it would be correlated
choices.why: Correlation is about referring outward, and a derived table may not do that anyway.

choices.text: It marks the subquery as independent
choices.why: Independence follows from what the subquery mentions, not from having a name.

choices.text: Its columns are named through it
choices.why: PostgreSQL and MySQL refuse one without a name; write it where SQLite would let you skip.

prompt: A subquery written where a single value is expected has to return one row and one ___.
hint: Two words describe the shape it is allowed to have, and you have one of them.

prompt: Where may a subquery not be written, in any engine you will meet?
hint: It is the clause that decides the piles.

choices.why: What you want there is a derived table with the expression inside and the grouping outside.
It takes a condition on a group, and that condition may contain a subquery.
A subquery is welcome there, and a correlated one is a common way to sort.

choices.text: The ON clause of a join
choices.why: A condition may contain a subquery like any other condition can.

prompt: What does EXISTS look at in its subquery's SELECT list?
hint: There is a reason SELECT 1 and SELECT * behave identically.

choices.why: There is no outer expression to match: EXISTS takes no left-hand side.
That is what IN does, and it is the difference between the two.
Something has to be written there, and every planner discards it.
No comparison is made out here, so no type has to be agreed.

prompt: Why does category_id NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) return no rows, whatever the table holds?
hint: Unfold it into the three comparisons it stands for.

choices.text: An AND with an unknown is not true
choices.why: The third comparison is unknown for any value, so the conjunction can never hold.

choices.text: The list is not valid SQL
choices.why: It is valid SQL and it is evaluated exactly as written.
A null matches no value at all, which is the opposite direction.

choices.text: The database stops at the first unknown
choices.why: It evaluates the condition per row and returns what the logic says.

prompt: Which of these is immune to that trap?
hint: Ask where the comparison actually happens in each one.

choices.text: NOT IN wrapped in a derived table
choices.why: Wrapping changes nothing about the logic of the membership test.

choices.text: NOT IN with coalesce on the column
choices.why: The null is in the set, not in the column being tested.
It spells it out and inherits the behaviour along with it.
The comparison is inside, one row at a time, and existence is true or false.

prompt: x > ALL (SELECT …) where the subquery returns no rows. What is the result?
hint: Empty sets are where these operators part company with intuition.

choices.why: The aggregate form does return null there, and that is the disagreement.
There is no row that fails the comparison, so the condition holds.
An empty set is an ordinary input, and the operator has an answer for it.
There was no row to satisfy it, and the operator reads that as nothing failing.

prompt: Match each form to what a null in the set does to it.
hint: Two of the three do their comparing one row at a time.

pairs.right: A null in the set empties the answer
Safe: the comparison happens per row
Safe: the pairing fails and the row is kept

right_distractors: Safe: the engine rewrites it into NOT EXISTS for you
A null in the set is discarded before the comparison

prompt: Somebody tells you EXISTS is faster than IN. What is the honest answer?
hint: The claim was true of something, once.

choices.text: IN wins, the set is built once
choices.why: A planner that builds a set does so for either spelling.

choices.text: They differ by engine, so write EXISTS
choices.why: They are equally portable, and portability is not what the claim was about.
In PostgreSQL both usually become the same semi-join; MySQL was bad at IN before 8.
Semi-joins stop early whichever way the query was written.

prompt: What makes a subquery correlated?
hint: Try running it on its own and see what stops you.

choices.text: It returns one row per outer row
choices.why: That is a consequence people expect, and it is not the definition.
EXISTS is usually correlated by habit, and IN can be correlated too.

choices.text: It sits in WHERE rather than FROM
choices.why: Both clauses take either kind, so position decides nothing.

choices.text: It refers to the outer query
choices.why: Paste it into a client by itself and it is a syntax error.

prompt: Three correlated subqueries over the same table, in one SELECT list. What is the rewrite?
hint: They are asking about the same rows three times.

choices.text: A UNION of the three, pivoted back
choices.why: That is more work to write and more work to run than the join.
Better than three correlated ones and still three passes over the table.

choices.text: One LEFT JOIN with a GROUP BY
choices.why: Three numbers in one pass, and count(o.id) rather than count(*) for lesson 6's reason.

choices.text: One correlated subquery returning three columns
choices.why: A scalar position takes one value, so three columns have nowhere to go.

prompt: A correlated subquery is quick in development and slow in production. What is the usual reason?
hint: Something that was happening quietly stopped happening.

choices.why: Stale statistics change plans, and they do not change how many rows match.
Whether the loop becomes a join depends on the engine, the version and the query.
Row width is a small constant factor, and this defect is a change of shape.

choices.text: The network between them is slower
choices.why: The subquery runs inside the database, so no iteration crosses a network.

prompt: UPDATE customers SET last_order_at = (SELECT max(…) …), with no WHERE. What is the risk?
hint: Think about the customers the subquery finds no rows for.

choices.text: Rows with no match are overwritten
choices.why: A customer whose orders were archived gets a null written over a value that was true.

choices.text: Rows with no match are skipped instead
choices.why: Every row is updated; the question is what the unmatched ones are updated to.
An aggregate over no rows is null, and writing a null is not a failure.
It mentions the outer row, so it is evaluated against each customer.

prompt: An application that loops over customers and runs one query per customer. How does that relate to this section?
hint: The shape is identical and the altitude is different.

choices.why: The flow is the same loop, moved somewhere that makes each step far dearer.

choices.text: It is safer, one transaction each
choices.why: Separate transactions make the set of results inconsistent rather than safe.

choices.text: It is the same thing over a network
choices.why: Lesson 11 calls it N+1; the database at least has a planner that might rescue its version.

choices.text: It is quicker, the application can cache
choices.why: A cache can help and the round trips are what dominates.

prompt: Why can a subquery in FROM not refer to a column of the query around it?
hint: Work out the order in which the two are evaluated.

choices.text: Its alias shadows the outer names
choices.why: An alias names the derived table and takes nothing away from the outer one.
The outer table does not exist yet when it runs, which is what LATERAL changes.
There is no ambiguity in the reference; there is simply no such table yet.
Materialisation is a choice the planner makes, and the restriction holds either way.

prompt: What does LATERAL do?
hint: It removes the restriction the previous question was about.

choices.text: Runs the inner query per outer row
choices.why: With that row's values available, which is how top N per group gets a LIMIT.
It is the opposite: the inner query is evaluated again for each outer row.

choices.text: Lets the outer query see its columns
choices.why: It already can: that is what the alias is for, and it is the other direction.

choices.text: Joins the two sides with no condition
choices.why: CROSS JOIN LATERAL looks like that and the inner query does see the outer row.

prompt: A filter outside a derived table is usually pushed inside. Where does the pushdown stop?
hint: It stops wherever pushing it through would change the answer.

choices.text: At a GROUP BY or a HAVING
choices.why: A filter on a grouping column is pushed through a GROUP BY quite happily.
Filters are pushed through joins routinely, and into either side.
Also at DISTINCT and at LIMIT, for the same reason in each case.
Sorting does not decide which rows exist, so a filter crosses it safely.

prompt: A query nested three levels deep says the same thing, and reads far better, once each step has a name. The keyword that gives it one is ___.
hint: One keyword, and it opens the next section.

prompt: Why write count(*) AS orders rather than count(*) inside a derived table?
hint: Ask what the outer query has to type to reach it.

choices.text: Without it the column is left out of SELECT *
choices.why: It appears in the star expansion under whatever name it was given.
It is accepted; the trouble arrives later, when something refers to it.

choices.text: The column needs a name you chose
choices.why: Otherwise it is whatever the engine calls it, and an upgrade can rename it.

choices.text: The alias is what allows the pushdown
choices.why: Pushdown is decided by the shape of the query, and names play no part.

prompt: Which other CTEs may a definition inside a WITH refer to?
hint: It is a sequence, read in the order it is written.

choices.why: Statements do not call each other, and a WITH lives inside one statement.
A later name is not visible to an earlier definition, so the steps go one way.
Referring forwards would make the order of the list meaningless.
The statement uses the CTEs; it is not something they can read from.

prompt: What does a WITH compute that a derived table does not?
hint: Compare the two versions of the same query in the section.

choices.text: A result cached for the session
choices.why: It lasts for one statement, and nothing carries it to the next.
Planning covers the whole statement at once, including the named steps.

choices.text: Nothing at all: the same thing
choices.why: The difference is readability, and being able to reuse a step without writing it twice.
Whether it is materialised is the planner's decision, not the keyword's.

prompt: A PostgreSQL statement has a DELETE … RETURNING in one CTE and a SELECT in another. What does the SELECT see?
hint: They look like steps and they are not.

choices.text: Whatever the order in the WITH decides
choices.why: The layout suggests a sequence and the engine does not promise one.
Written order is not run order, and the run order is undefined.

choices.text: The data as it was before either ran
choices.why: Every part sees one snapshot; two parts that modify the same row are unreasonable.
It is accepted, which is what makes the snapshot rule worth knowing.

prompt: Which engines refuse INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE inside a WITH?
hint: One of them is where the feature is best known.

choices.why: MariaDB had it from 10.2, and it is not the odd one out here.
There it is two statements in a transaction, which is the next lesson.
PostgreSQL is the engine where the feature is most developed.
A CTE has to be a query, and in PostgreSQL a writing statement counts.

prompt: The steps in a WITH are named t1, t2 and sub. What has been given up?
hint: The names were the feature.

choices.why: If the list of names does not describe the query, it is a nested query with labels.
Inlining is decided from the shape and the reference count, not the spelling.
A badly named step can still be referenced twice.
They do not reach the engine, and the engine was never who they were for.

prompt: What are the two halves of a recursive CTE?
hint: One says where to begin and one says how to go further.

choices.text: A base case and a return value
choices.why: Nothing calls itself here; the name is misleading and the shape is a loop.
No rows are inserted anywhere: the result is the rounds stacked together.

choices.text: An anchor and a repeating step
choices.why: With UNION ALL between them, and the step joins against what came before.

choices.text: A forward pass and a backward pass
choices.why: One direction is all a given query walks; reversing it is a different query.

prompt: Each round of the recursion joins against which rows?
hint: This is the reason the query terminates.

choices.text: The anchor's rows, again each round
choices.why: The anchor runs once; joining against it again would never go past level two.
The join is against the recursive name, and that name holds one round.
That would revisit the same rows for ever on a tree of any depth.
A round that adds no rows ends the query, and the rounds are stacked as the result.

prompt: How do you turn "everything under this category" into "everything above it"?
hint: One line of the query changes.

choices.why: That changes how duplicates are treated and leaves the direction alone.
Sorting the same rows differently does not fetch a different set of rows.
The anchor says where to start, and both directions start at the same place.

choices.text: Swap the sides of the join
choices.why: a.parent_id = c.id instead of c.parent_id = t.id, and the rest stands.

prompt: Why is UNION in place of UNION ALL a poor defence against a cycle?
hint: It does stop the query. Ask what it costs and what it teaches.

choices.text: It is unsupported in a recursive query
choices.why: It is supported, and the standard describes both forms.

choices.text: It hides that the data has a cycle
choices.why: And deduplicating every round is expensive on a large tree.

choices.text: It does not make it terminate sooner
choices.why: Deduplicating is exactly what makes it terminate, which is why people reach for it.
The anchor is unaffected; the deduplication applies to what the rounds add.

prompt: Why would a report generate a row per day with a recursive CTE before joining the data on?
hint: Lesson 6 said something about a group with no rows.

choices.text: Grouping on a date is not deterministic
choices.why: Grouping on a date is as deterministic as grouping on anything else.

choices.text: date_trunc will not invent a month
choices.why: Truncation works on the rows it is given, and it is not what is missing here.

choices.text: So an index on the date is used
choices.why: An index is about finding rows that exist, and the trouble is the ones that do not.

choices.text: So a day with no sales shows a zero
choices.why: A group is made of rows, so a day with no sales has no group to appear as.

prompt: To sort a tree so that each child sits directly under its parent, carry an accumulated ___ down the recursion and sort by it.
hint: An array in PostgreSQL, a string everywhere else.

prompt: What did PostgreSQL do with a CTE before version 12?
hint: It was known as a fence, which is a hint about what it stopped.

choices.why: That rule is the new one, and before it there was no decision to make.

choices.text: Refused it without a GROUP BY
choices.why: There was no such restriction in any version.
So no filter from outside could be pushed in, and a lookup read the whole table.
Inlining is what version 12 introduced as the usual case.

prompt: From PostgreSQL 12, when is a CTE inlined?
hint: Three conditions, and one of them is about counting.

choices.text: When a filter could be pushed down
choices.why: The pushdown is the benefit of inlining, and it is not the test for it.
Aggregates are ordinary, and a CTE full of them is inlined like any other.
And is not recursive, and modifies no data; otherwise it is materialised.
That keyword asks for the opposite of inlining.

prompt: A CTE referenced twice, on PostgreSQL 15. Is its body computed twice?
hint: Apply the rule from the previous question and see what falls out.

choices.why: Inlining would compute it twice, so the rule leaves it alone — a consequence, not a promise.
Inlining applies to a CTE referenced once, and this one is referenced twice.
The count is what the rule looks at, and where they appear does not enter it.
That keyword asks for inlining, which is the version that would compute it twice.

prompt: You want a step fenced off from the outer query, on purpose. What do you write?
hint: Say what you mean rather than relying on a version's default.

choices.why: And a comment saying why, or the next person rewrites it and the plan changes.
It asks for inlining, which is the thing a fence is meant to prevent.
True, and rewriting a step as a recursion to get a fence is a poor trade.

choices.text: No keyword: a CTE is a fence
choices.why: It was in PostgreSQL 11 and it is not in PostgreSQL 12.

prompt: Advice about CTE performance written in 2017 describes what?
hint: Ask what changed, and when.

choices.why: The rule it describes was replaced, which is why the advice reads so confidently.
MySQL had no CTEs at all until 8.0, which arrived in 2018.
Version 12 changed the default in 2019, and nothing on the internet is revised.

choices.text: Recursive CTEs, slow then and now
choices.why: A recursive CTE is materialised in either era, so nothing about it changed.

prompt: What does CREATE VIEW store?
hint: The word in the section title is the answer.

choices.why: That describes the other kind, which is the last section of this lesson.

choices.text: The rows, refreshed as data changes
choices.why: Keeping a copy current is work that something would have to be doing.

choices.text: The query as it was written
choices.why: It is substituted and run every time, against the data as it is at that moment.
Plans are made per statement, and a view is expanded before planning.

prompt: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT * FROM products, and later a column is added to products. What does SELECT * FROM v show?
hint: Ask when the star was turned into a list.

choices.text: The columns it had that day
choices.why: The star was expanded at creation, and there is no error and no notice.

choices.text: The new column, from next read
choices.why: There is no moment at which the view re-expands its own star.
It is a query whose column list was fixed when the query was stored.
Nothing is checked at read time, which is why this is easy to miss.

prompt: An UPDATE through a view sets a value that the view's own WHERE excludes. What happens by default?
hint: There is a clause you can add to change this, which tells you the default.

choices.text: It succeeds and the row leaves
choices.why: It is no longer visible through the view, and WITH CHECK OPTION is what refuses it instead.
That is the behaviour you opt into, and it is not what you get for free.

choices.text: It succeeds and the view rebuilds
choices.why: A view has nothing to rebuild: it holds a definition and no rows.

choices.text: The view changes, not the table
choices.why: There is nowhere else for the write to land.

prompt: SELECT * FROM summary_view WHERE id = 7 takes nine seconds. What is the likely reason?
hint: The same thing that stops a filter reaching into a derived table.

choices.text: The view has no index of its own
choices.why: Indexes belong to the tables underneath, and a fast view uses them.
Plain views hold no rows, so there is nothing to refresh.
A DISTINCT, a window or a GROUP BY that the condition cannot be pushed through.

choices.text: It is planned from scratch each time
choices.why: Planning a statement is milliseconds, and the expansion is routine.

prompt: What is the strongest argument for a view?
hint: It has little to do with the database.

choices.text: Keeping a copy aside for reporting
choices.why: A view keeps no copy, so there is nothing set aside.
That is the other kind of view, and it comes with staleness attached.
"Active customer" written into four reports is written four different ways.
Plans are not what a view holds, and they are cheap to make.

prompt: A plain view is used to hide columns from a role. What can still leak rows?
hint: Something the reader can put in the WHERE that runs before the view's own conditions.

choices.text: A cheap function in the WHERE
choices.why: The planner may evaluate it first; security_barrier or row-level security is the answer.

choices.text: An ORDER BY on a hidden one
choices.why: A column the view does not expose cannot be named in the outer query.

choices.text: Granting on the view, not the table
choices.why: That is the arrangement being described, and it is the point of it.

choices.text: A join added to the outer query
choices.why: A join reaches other tables, and the grants on those are checked as usual.

prompt: What is different about a materialised view?
hint: One word changed in the CREATE statement.

choices.text: It recomputes when a base table changes
choices.why: Nothing watches the base tables; a refresh is something somebody runs.
Some ordinary views accept writes and some do not, which is a separate question.

choices.text: It keeps a plan for later
choices.why: Plans are not what either kind of view keeps.
Reading it reads stored data, however long the query underneath took to run.

prompt: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, without CONCURRENTLY. What happens to somebody reading it?
hint: The statement takes an exclusive lock.

choices.text: They wait for it to finish
choices.why: On a big view that is minutes of a dashboard with nothing on it.
The read is held rather than refused.
A reader is never shown a half-built result.
That is what CONCURRENTLY buys, and it is what the plain form lacks.

prompt: What does REFRESH … CONCURRENTLY require?
hint: It has to work out which rows changed.

choices.text: A primary key on the base table
choices.why: The index has to be on the view itself, where the matching happens.

choices.text: A unique index on the view
choices.why: Without one it has no way to match old rows against new; it is slower and worth it.

choices.text: A view created WITH NO DATA
choices.why: That option governs the first population and has no bearing here.
Avoiding that lock is the entire purpose of the option.

prompt: Three questions to ask of a materialised view. Which is the one people forget?
hint: The other two get asked while the thing is being built.

choices.text: What happens when the refresh fails
choices.why: Serving last Tuesday's number as today's beats no number for as long as nobody checks.

choices.text: Which job refreshes it, and how often
choices.why: It gets asked, because something has to be written for it to happen at all.

choices.text: Which column should carry an index
choices.why: A fair question, and it is about speed rather than about truth.

choices.text: How stale the numbers may be
choices.why: It gets asked, and it is answered by whoever reads the report.

prompt: A query is slow. What comes before caching its answer in a materialised view?
hint: Two lessons are named in the section, in an order.

choices.why: That improves the cache you have not yet justified building.
It reduces the symptom for the people who notice it and changes nothing else.
Naming the steps helps a reader and moves no work off the machine.

choices.text: Finding out why it is slow
choices.why: A missing index costs one statement; a cache costs a job, a staleness window and a failure mode.
